5 Number of times the bowler took 5 or more wickets in an innings

When did each country first play internationally?

From the earliest debut years of players, it could be seen when each format was started and when each country started playing in a format. Australia and England have been the pioneering nations in each format. The earliest Tests were played between Australia and England in 1877. South Africa joined the fray in 1889. For the next 40 years, these were the only 3 international teams, until West Indies, India and New Zealand started playing in quick succession. In 1970 South Africa was suspended from playing international cricket by the ICC because of prevailing apartheid in the nation. As a result, the international career of some very promising South Africans like Graeme Pollock and Barry Richards ended abruptly. Later on some other players emigrated to England and Australia to get a chance to play internationally. This ban was lifted by the ICC in 1991. The newly formed South African team under Clive Rice was given a warm welcome in India, when they visited to play ODIs. South Africa resumed playing tests in 1992.

Sri Lanka, Zimbabwe and Bangladesh were Associate members with ODI status before they were elected as full members to be eligible to play Tests.


Number of players who have represented their country internationally

Even though Australia and England started playing Tests together in 1877, there have been far more players representing the England team in Tests, when looking at the entire history. This suggests a lot more turnover in the English team.


Number of players who debuted internationally by year

This plot shows the number of distinct players debuting each year. So, for instance, if a player debuted in Tests, ODIs and T20Is team in the same year, then that is counted as 1. Few things could be noted here:

  • The gaps in Australia, England and India facets show the years interrupted by the 2 world wars.
  • As noted earlier, there’s a big gap in the South Africa facet, when the country was suspended from 1970-1991.
  • The gaps in Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Zimbabwe are because each country was an associate member of the ICC and was only competing in ICC ODI tournaments until the country got its full member status.
  • There’s been a steady increase in the number of players debuting in Australia, England, India, Pakistan and West Indies, in the last decade or so. This suggests a trend of having specialist players in the team for each format. Top teams like Australia, England and India have adopted this trend. Some players are selected as Test match specialists, while the others are selected to only play in ODIs and T20Is.

Career spans of players

To examine the career spans of players, I filtered the dataset to only keep the players who haven’t been active in 2016-2017. Then I eliminated quick failures whose career didn’t last for more than 2 years. This meant the players left in the dataset were given enough opportunities to succeed at the international level. Then I examined the median career span by debut year.

It appears a median player used to play between 6 to 10 years before retiring. Although there was more dispersion in Tests, it was clearly the norm in ODIs. 1908 was an extreme outlier year in Tests because only 1 player qualified the inclusion criteria. This was Sir Jack Hobbs of England, an early master of the game who played for 23 years. 1909 was another extreme outlier year where only 3 players were included. These were the legends Warren Bardsley of Australia (18 years), Frank Woolley of England (26 years) and Bill Whitty of Australia (4 years).

An outlier in the ODIs plot corresponds to the year 1989. This was the year when some modern day legends made their debut. Most notably Sachin Tendulkar from India who played for 24 years. Saeed Anwar, Waqar Younis & Mushtaq Ahmed from Pakistan who each played for 15 years and Sanath Jayasuriya from Sri Lanka who played for 23 years. Alec Stewart and Nasser Hussain from England also debuted in 1989. They had checkered records in ODIs but overall their careers lasted for 15 years.

An astonishing trend appears to have started with the players debuting after the early 90s. Career spans of players peaked with those debuting during early 90s. Since then the median career span started dropping year by year. This could be seen across all formats. Although the median career span would change for more recent years as active players playing from early 2000s retire in future, nevertheless this trend is persistent from early 90s.

Matches played by debut years

The same downwards trends from early 90s could also be observed in the median number of matches played by debut year. This isn’t surprising as the number of matches played is directly correlated with career span. An upward trend from early 30s could be observed in Test matches played. This is explained by the addition of West Indies, New Zealand and India as full members of the ICC from late 20s. Every international player started playing more matches as the number of competing teams doubled to 6.

A big upward trend could be seen in ODIs from its inception. Until the beginning of ODIs, cricket was only played in Tests format that was characteristically very laid back. Both teams got a chance to bat upto 2 innings alternately over 5 days. More often than not the matches would end in a draw with no win/loss result. The introduction of 60 overs a side ODIs (later reduced to 50 overs a side) format was to be played in a single day. The team batting first would set a target score. Then the team batting second would chase this target. This ensured guaranteed results although there have been few occasions where the ODIs have resulted in ties at the same score. Naturally this format was more palatable to spectators and TV audiences that contributed to a rapid growth in its popularity. The ODIs format is still the most popular format till date.

In the next couple of posts I will analyze batting performances.

item.title: Ames Housing - Part 2 - Building Models
item.description:
In a previous post in this series, we did an exploratory data analysis of the Ames Housing dataset.

In this post, we will build both linear and non-linear models and see how well they predict the SalePrice of properties.

Evaluation Criteria

Root-Mean-Squared-Error (RMSE) between the logarithm of the predicted value and the logarithm of the observed SalePrice will be our evaluation criteria. Taking the log ensures that errors in predicting expensive and cheap houses will affect the result equally.

Steps for Building Models

Here are the steps for building models and determining the best hyperparameter combinations by K-fold cross validation:

  • Partition the training dataset into model training and validation sets. Use stratified sampling such that each partition has a similar distribution of the target variable - SalePrice.
  • Define linear and non-linear models.
  • For each model, create a space-filling (maximum entropy) grid of hyperparameter combinations.
  • For each hyperparameter combination, fit a model on the training set and make predictions on the validation set. Repeat the process for all folds.
  • Determine root mean squared errors (RMSE) and choose the best hyperparameter combination that corresponds to the minimum RMSE.
  • Train each model with its best hyperparameter combination on the entire training set.
  • Calculate RMSE of the each finalized model on the testing set.
  • Finally, choose the best model that gives the least RMSE.

Partitioning Training Data

We split the training data into 5 folds. Within each fold, 80% of the data is used for training models and 20% for validating the predicted values against the actual values.

Let’s look at the distribution of the target variable across all folds:

cv_folds %>% 
  mutate(target = map(splits, function(Z) bind_rows(training(Z) %>% select(target) %>% mutate(type = "training"), 
                                                    testing(Z) %>% select(target) %>% mutate(type = "validation")))) %>% 
  select(-splits) %>% 
  unnest(cols = c(target)) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = target)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, color = "white", fill = "#F37735") +
  labs(x = "log(SalePrice)") +
  facet_grid(type ~ id)

By using stratified sampling, we ensure that the training and validation distributions of the target variable are similar.

Linear Models

Ordinary Least Squares Regression

Before creating any new features or indulging in more complex modelling methods, we will cross validate a simple linear model on the training data to establish a benchmark. If more complex approaches do not have a significant improvement in the model validation metrics, then they are not worthwhile to be pursued.

model_spec_lm

Computational engine: lm

# A tibble: 1 × 1

      <dbl>
1     0.147
rmse_val <- cv_results_lm %>% pull(mean_rmse)

What’s notable?

  • After training a linear model on all predictors, we get an RMSE of 0.1468.
  • This is the simplest and fastest model with no hyperparameters to tune.

Regularized Linear Model

We will use glmnet that uses LASSO and Ridge Regression with regularization. We will do a grid search of the following hyperparameters that minimize RMSE:

  • penalty: The total amount of regularization in the model.
  • mixture: The proportion of L1 regularization in the model.

 7 1.15e- 4  0.798      0.138
 8 7.37e- 7  0.0221     0.138
 9 1.23e-10  0.333      0.138
10 2.07e- 9  0.950      0.138

What’s notable?

  • After hyperparameter tuning with cross validation, the best glmnet model gives an RMSE of 0.128 with penalty = 0.0146 and mixture = 0.2974.
  • It is a significant improvement over Ordinary Least Squares regression that had an RMSE of 0.1468.
  • glmnet cross validation is fast, taking about 13 seconds to execute.
  • But the presence of outliers can significantly affect its performance.

Here a plot of the glmnet hyperparameter grid along with the best hyperparameter combination:

eda_plot_scatter(param_grid_glmnet, "mixture", "penalty", alpha = 1, add_lm = F, yLog = T, yLabelsScale = scales::scientific) +
  geom_point(data = param_best_glmnet, aes(x = mixture, y = penalty), color = "red") +
  ggrepel::geom_label_repel(data = param_best_glmnet %>% map_df(round, digits = 4), 
                            aes(x = mixture, y = penalty, label = glue::glue("penalty: {penalty}, mixture:{mixture}")),
                            family = "Roboto Condensed")

Non-linear Models

Next, we will train a couple of tree-based algorithms, which are not very sensitive to outliers and skewed data.

ranger (Random Forest)

We use the ranger implementation of random forests, which gives the same results as the randomForest package but runs about 3 times faster. In each ensemble, we have 500 trees (random forest error levels off well before that on a dataset of this size) and do a grid search of the following hyperparameters:

  • mtry: The number of predictors to randomly sample at each split.
  • min_n: The minimum number of data points in a node required to further split the node.
model_spec_rf
Random Forest Model Specification (regression)

Main Arguments:
  mtry = tune()
  trees = 500
  min_n = tune()

Engine-Specific Arguments:
  num.threads = 1

Computational engine: ranger

Let’s take a look at the top 10 RMSE values and hyperparameter combinations:

cv_results_rf %>% head(10)
# A tibble: 10 × 3
   min_n  mtry mean_rmse
   <int> <int>     <dbl>
 1     2    84     0.134
 2     5   134     0.136
 3     9    36     0.136
 4    12   110     0.136
 5    15    55     0.136
 6    18   136     0.137
 7     8   199     0.138
 8    22    69     0.138
 9    19   179     0.139
10    29   123     0.139

What’s notable?

  • After cross validation, we get the best RMSE of 0.134 with mtry = 84 and min_n = 2.
  • This is no improvement in RMSE compared to glmnet, and ranger cross validation takes much longer to execute (about 371 seconds, versus 13 seconds for glmnet).

Here a plot of the ranger hyperparameter grid along with the best hyperparameter combination:

eda_plot_scatter(param_grid_rf, "min_n", "mtry", alpha = 1, add_lm = F) +
  geom_point(data = param_best_rf, aes(x = min_n, y = mtry), color = "red") +
  ggrepel::geom_label_repel(data = param_best_rf, aes(x = min_n, y = mtry, label = glue::glue("mtry: {mtry}, min_n:{min_n}")), family = "Roboto Condensed")

xgboost

In each ensemble we have 1000 trees and do a grid search of the following hyperparameters:

  • min_n: The minimum number of data points in a node required to further split the node.
  • tree_depth: The maximum depth or the number of splits of the tree.
  • learn_rate: The rate at which the boosting algorithm adapts from one iteration to another.
model_spec_xgboost
Boosted Tree Model Specification (regression)

Main Arguments:
  trees = 1000
  min_n = tune()
  tree_depth = tune()
  learn_rate = tune()

Engine-Specific Arguments:
  objective = reg:squarederror
  nthread = 1

Computational engine: xgboost

Let’s take a look at the top 10 RMSE values and hyperparameter combinations:

cv_results_xgboost %>% head(10)
# A tibble: 10 × 4
   min_n tree_depth learn_rate mean_rmse
   <int>      <int>      <dbl>     <dbl>
 1    33          2    0.0289      0.126
 2    23          4    0.0254      0.127
 3     3          2    0.0171      0.127
 4    24          1    0.190       0.128
 5    38          9    0.0270      0.130
 6     4          1    0.0872      0.131

 8    32          9    0.00605     0.131
 9    19         11    0.00482     0.131
10    11          5    0.0549      0.131

What’s notable?

  • After cross validation, we get the best RMSE of 0.126 with min_n = 33, tree_depth = 2 and learn_rate = 0.0289.
  • This is the best cross validated RMSE of all the models, slightly ahead of glmnet (0.128) and ranger (0.134).
  • xgboost cross validation takes longer to execute than that of glmnet, but is faster than that of ranger (about 168 seconds).

Finalizing Models

For each model, we found the combination of hyperparameters that minimize RMSE. Using those parameters, we can now train the same models on the entire training dataset. Finally, we can use the trained models to predict log(SalePrice) on the entire training set to see the actual v/s predicted log(SalePrice) results.

# Get predicted estimates
get_predicted <- function(model_final, dfNew) {

  # Predict on testing set
  vEstimates <- model_final %>%
    predict(new_data = dfNew) %>%
    pull(.pred)
  
  return(vEstimates)
}

dfResults_train <- dfTrain %>% 
  mutate(actual = log(SalePrice)) %>% 
  select(Id, actual) %>% 
  mutate(glmnet = get_predicted(model_final = model_final_glmnet, dfTrain_Proc),
         ranger = get_predicted(model_final = model_final_rf, dfTrain_Proc),
         xgboost = get_predicted(model_final = model_final_xgboost, dfTrain_Proc))
dfPlot <- dfResults_train %>% 
  gather(model, predicted, -actual, -Id) %>% 
  mutate(model = ordered(model, levels = c("glmnet","ranger","xgboost")))

dfPlot %>%
  rename(`log(SalePrice)` = actual) %>%
  eda_plot_actual_vs_predicted("log(SalePrice)", "predicted", feature_model = "model", feature_id = "Id", nLabel = 3) +
  labs(title = "Actual v/s predicted log(SalePrice) on training set")

# properties among the 3 largest errors of every model
vWorst_train <- dfPlot %>% 
  group_by(model) %>% 
  slice_max(abs(predicted - actual), n = 3) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  count(Id) %>% 
  filter(n == n_distinct(dfPlot$model)) %>% 
  pull(Id)

What’s notable?

  • Both ranger and xgboost models fit the training data closely with the tuned parameters, as the predictions lie close to the straight line drawn at 45 degrees. ranger fits it most closely, with a training RMSE of 0.051 versus 0.094 for xgboost.
  • The glmnet model shows a couple of outliers with Ids 524 and 1299 whose predicted values are far in excess of their actual values. Even properties whose SalePrice is at the lower end, show a wide dispersion in prediced values.
  • The plots label the three largest errors of each model. The property with Id 633 is among them for all three models, so it is worth checking for errors in its data.
  • But the true performance can only be measured on unseen testing data.

Performance on Test Data

dfResults_test <- dfTest %>% 
  mutate(actual = log(SalePrice)) %>% 
  select(Id, actual) %>% 
  mutate(glmnet = get_predicted(model_final = model_final_glmnet, dfTest_Proc),
         ranger = get_predicted(model_final = model_final_rf, dfTest_Proc),
         xgboost = get_predicted(model_final = model_final_xgboost, dfTest_Proc))
dfPlot <- dfResults_test %>% 
  gather(model, predicted, -actual, -Id) %>% 
  mutate(model = ordered(model, levels = c("glmnet","ranger","xgboost")))

dfPlot %>%
  rename(`log(SalePrice)` = actual) %>%
  eda_plot_actual_vs_predicted("log(SalePrice)", "predicted", feature_model = "model", feature_id = "Id", nLabel = 3) +
  labs(title = "Actual v/s predicted log(SalePrice) on testing set")

dfRMSE <- map(list("glmnet","ranger","xgboost"), ~ rmse(dfResults_test, actual, !!sym(.x)) %>% mutate(model = .x)) %>%
  bind_rows() %>%
  mutate(cv_rmse = c(cv_results_glmnet$mean_rmse[1], cv_results_rf$mean_rmse[1], cv_results_xgboost$mean_rmse[1])) %>%
  select(-.estimator, -.metric) %>%
  rename(test_rmse = .estimate) %>%
  select(model, everything())

dfRMSE
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  model   test_rmse cv_rmse
  <chr>       <dbl>   <dbl>
1 glmnet      0.130   0.128
2 ranger      0.138   0.134
3 xgboost     0.131   0.126

What’s notable?

  • All models have similar RMSE on the unseen testing set as their cross validated RMSE, which shows the cross validation process and hyperparameters worked very well.
  • Records with Ids 1537 and 2217 are outliers, as none of the models are able to predict close to actual values.
  • glmnet has the lowest test RMSE of 0.130, with xgboost close behind at 0.131.
  • However, glmnet is sensitive to outliers, as we saw with Ids 524 and 1299 in the training set. Since xgboost had the best cross validated RMSE and the difference in test RMSE is small, we could finalize xgboost, which is robust to outliers and captures non-linear relationships, as the model that generalizes well on this dataset.
model_final <- model_final_xgboost

Feature Importance

Even though xgboost is not as easily interpretable as a linear model, we could use variable importance plots to determine the most important features selected by the model.

Let’s take a look at the top 10 most important features of our finalized xgboost model:

library(vip)

p1 <- vip(extract_fit_parsnip(model_final), aesthetics = list(fill = "#00AED8")) +
  labs(title = "xgboost model Feature Importance in Training") +
  theme_quant()

vFeaturesImp <- vip::vi(extract_fit_parsnip(model_final)) %>% top_n(10, Importance) %>% pull(Variable)

p2 <- eda_plot_correlation_matrix(dfTrain %>% select(SalePrice, one_of(vFeaturesImp)), 
                            outlineVar = "SalePrice", plotTitle = "Correlations with SalePrice")

cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = list(p1, p2), nrow = 1)

  • Correlations of numerical features are plotted side-by-side. All of them have a correlation of 0.5 or more (in absolute terms) with SalePrice.
  • All of the top 10 features make sense. To evaluate SalePrice, a buyer would definitely look at total square footage, overall quality, neighborhood, number of bathrooms, kitchen quality, age of property, garage size and finish, central air conditioning, fireplace quality, etc.
  • This shows, our finalized model generalizes well and makes very reasonable choices in terms of features.

New Property Premium

Among the top 10 features by importance in our final model, most of the features like square footage, neighborhood and number of bathrooms remain the same throughout the life of the property. Quality and condition of property does change but their evaluation is mostly subjective. The only other feature that cannot be disputed to change over time is PropertyAge.

So, how would the predicted SalePrice differ if a property was newly constructed vis-a-vis the same property if it were constructed more than 30 years earlier, and all the times in between?

We could pick a couple of properties at random, change PropertyAge and see its impact on SalePrice.

getSampleProperty <- function(randomSeed) {
  
  set.seed(randomSeed)
  dfSample <- dfTest %>% 
    filter(PropertyAge >= 30) %>% 
    sample_n(1)
  
  dfSample <- tibble(PropertyAge = 1:dfSample$PropertyAge[1]) %>% expand_grid(dfSample %>% select(-PropertyAge))
}

dfSample <- getSampleProperty(1000) %>% bind_rows(getSampleProperty(2000))

# preprocess the sample data and generated predicted values from the final model
get_preprocessing_recipe(dfSample) %>% 
  bake(dfSample) %>% 
  get_predicted(model_final, .) %>% 
  as_tibble() %>% 
  bind_cols(dfSample) %>% 
  mutate(predicted = exp(value)) %>% 
  group_by(Id) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = PropertyAge, y = predicted)) +
  geom_point(color = "#00AED8") +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~Id, scales = "free") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(y = "Predicted Sale Price",
       title = "New Property Premium")

We can see there’s a small premium for a newly constructed property v/s an older property of the same build, quality and condition. This premium isn’t very much in a place like Ames, IA but we’d reckon it would be much higher in a larger metropolitan city.

  mutate(Functional = factor(Functional, levels = c("Typ", "Min1", "Min2", "Mod", "Maj1", "Maj2", "Sev", "Sal"), ordered = TRUE)) %>% 
  mutate(GarageFinish = factor(GarageFinish, levels = c("Fin", "RFn", "Unf", "None"), ordered = TRUE)) %>% 
  mutate(Street = factor(Street, levels = c("Pave","Grvl"), ordered = TRUE)) %>% 
  mutate(PavedDrive = factor(PavedDrive, levels = c("Y","P","N"), ordered = TRUE)) %>% 
  mutate(OverallCond = ordered(OverallCond, levels = 1:10),
         OverallQual = ordered(OverallQual, levels = 1:10)) %>% 
  mutate(CentralAir = ordered(CentralAir, levels = c("Y","N")),
         HasGarage = ordered(HasGarage, levels = c("TRUE", "FALSE")),
         HasFireplace = ordered(HasFireplace, levels = c("TRUE", "FALSE")),
         HasMasVnr = ordered(HasMasVnr, levels = c("TRUE", "FALSE")),
         HasPorch = ordered(HasPorch, levels = c("TRUE", "FALSE")),
         IsNew = ordered(IsNew, levels = c("TRUE","FALSE")),
         IsRemod = ordered(IsRemod, levels = c("TRUE","FALSE"))) %>% 
  # mutate_if(is.ordered, fct_rev) %>% # reverse the factor levels before assigning an integer order
  # mutate_if(is.ordered, function(Z) as.integer(Z) - 1) %>% 
  mutate_if(is.character, as.factor) %>% 
  mutate_if(is.nominal, ~ fct_lump_min(.x, min = 10)) %>% 
  mutate_if(is.logical, as.factor)

Features to Drop

Highly Correlated Features

Some features could be dropped from further analysis because either they are too correlated or replaced by a similar feature.

(vFeatures_to_exclude <- c("BsmtFullBath","GarageCars","GarageYrBlt",
                           "GrLivArea","PoolArea",
                           "YearBuilt","YearRemodAdd","Neighborhood",
                           "OpenPorchSF","EnclosedPorch","3SsnPorch","ScreenPorch"))
 [1] "BsmtFullBath"  "GarageCars"    "GarageYrBlt"   "GrLivArea"     "PoolArea"      "YearBuilt"     "YearRemodAdd"  "Neighborhood"  "OpenPorchSF"  
[10] "EnclosedPorch" "3SsnPorch"     "ScreenPorch"

Skewed Categorical Features

Any feature where more than 95% of the records have the same category probably doesn’t have any predictive value. An extreme case is Utilities which has only 2 categories - AllPub and NoSeWa in the dataset. Only 1 record has NoSeWa and the rest of the records have AllPub. Therefore, features like these do not have any predictive value.

Let’s see the share of the most common category in every categorical feature, along with the number of rare categories that have fewer than 10 records:

p_dominance <- eda_plot_category_dominance(dfClean, threshold = 0.95, minCount = 10)
p_dominance

dfDominance <- p_dominance$data
dfRare <- dfDominance %>% filter(share < 0.95, n_rare > 0) %>% arrange(desc(n_rare), desc(share))
  • 11 features lie above the 95% line, so we will drop them. These are plotted below.
  • Among the remaining features, 13 have at least one rare category with fewer than 10 records, such as Functional, GarageQual, Electrical. When these features are dummy encoded for modelling, the rare categories become predictors that are based on only a handful of records, so their effects cannot be estimated reliably. Combining rare categories into a single category is one way to deal with them.
vFeatures_skewed <- dfClean %>% 
  select_if(is.factor) %>% 
  gather(feature, value) %>% 
  group_by(feature, value) %>% 
  count() %>% 
  mutate(perc = n/nrow(dfClean)) %>% 
  dplyr::filter(perc > 0.95) %>% 
  pull(feature)

cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = map(vFeatures_skewed, ~ eda_plot_column(dfClean, .x)))

# Features to exclude for modelling
vFeatures_to_exclude <- c(vFeatures_to_exclude, vFeatures_skewed) %>% unique()

# cleanup
rm(vFeatures_skewed)

Finalized Data

# print("Following features are dropped")
# print(vFeatures_to_exclude)

# Finalized dataset
dfClean <- dfClean %>% select(-one_of(vFeatures_to_exclude))

# determine the numerical features
vFeaturesNum <- dfClean %>% select(-Id) %>% select_if(is.numeric) %>% colnames() %>% sort()

# determine the categorical features
vFeaturesCat <- dfClean %>% select(-Id) %>% select_if(is.factor) %>% colnames() %>% sort()
# vFeaturesCat1 <- vFeaturesCat[map_int(vFeaturesCat, ~ length(levels(dfClean[[.x]]))) > 5]
vFeaturesCat1 <- dfClean %>% select_if(is.ordered) %>% colnames() %>% sort()
vFeaturesCat2 <- setdiff(vFeaturesCat, vFeaturesCat1)

print("Dimensions of the finalized dataset")
[1] "Dimensions of the finalized dataset"
dim(dfClean)
[1] 2919   73
print(glue::glue("Excluding Id, there are {(ncol(dfClean)-1)} features in the finalized dataset."))
Excluding Id, there are 72 features in the finalized dataset.
print(glue::glue("There are {length(vFeaturesNum)} numerical, {length(vFeaturesCat1)} ordinal and {length(vFeaturesCat2)} nominal features."))
There are 26 numerical, 26 ordinal and 20 nominal features.

Univariate Analysis

Let us look at each feature in the dataset in detail.

Numerical Features

First let’s plot all the features that are measured as area in square feet:

eda_plot_histograms(dfClean, vFeaturesNum[str_detect(vFeaturesNum, "SF|Area")])

What’s notable?

  • All area features have outliers.
  • Many features are heavily skewed so they need to be normalized before fitting models.

Now let’s see other numerical features:

eda_plot_histograms(dfClean, setdiff(vFeaturesNum[!str_detect(vFeaturesNum, "SF|Area")], "SalePrice"))

What’s notable?

  • Most of the properties have been built less than 20 years prior to their sale.

Let’s plot the distribution of SalePrice in log scale:

eda_plot_histograms(dfClean, "SalePrice", nBins = 50, xLog = T, xLabelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1))

What’s notable?

  • We see long tailed distribution on both sides.
  • There are 11 properties below USD 50,000 and 17 above USD 500,000.
  • Linear models are very sensitive to the presence of outliers.

Categorical Features

Ordinal Features

cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = map(vFeaturesCat1, ~ eda_plot_column(dfClean, .x)), ncol = 4)

What’s notable?

  • Categorical imbalances exist in many features where 1 or 2 categories are dominant. This poses a big challenge for using these features as predictors, as categories with fewer counts tend to be underrepresented in the data.

Nominal Features.

cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = map(vFeaturesCat2, ~ eda_plot_column(dfClean, .x)), ncol = 4)

What’s notable?

  • Categorical imbalances exist in many features where 1 or 2 categories are dominant.
  • Most of the properties are sold during the summer months, and the least during the winter months.
  • The effect of housing market crisis are visible in the data, as the fewest properties were sold in 2010.

Bivariate Analysis

Numerical-Numerical

Let’s examine the relationship of SalePrice with other numerical features:

eda_plot_scatter(dfClean, vFeaturesNum, "SalePrice", yLabelsScale = scales::dollar)

vOutliers_TotalSF <- dfClean %>% filter(TotalSF > 7000) %>% pull(Id)

What’s notable?

  • From the scatterplot of TotalSF v/s SalePrice, it is very clear there are high leverage points where the target SalePrice is unusually low relative to the area in sq. ft. These points have an outsized impact on the slope of the regression line, which otherwise would be higher.
  • The same set of points impact TotalBsmtSF.
  • The Ids of these records are 524,1299,2550. Out of these 524 and 1299 are in the training set.

Transforming Skewed Features

Many numerical features are right skewed. Would transforming them make their relationship with log(SalePrice) more linear? Let’s compare common transforms of the strongest area feature TotalSF, the heavily skewed LotArea, and GarageArea, which is barely skewed. Each panel is labelled with the R-squared of a linear fit of log(SalePrice) on the transformed feature:

lTransformPlots <- map(c("TotalSF", "LotArea", "GarageArea"), ~ eda_plot_transforms(dfClean, .x, "SalePrice"))
cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = lTransformPlots, ncol = 1)

# R-squared of each transform, in the order of the panels
vR2 <- map(lTransformPlots, ~ .x$data %>%
             distinct(transform, r_squared) %>%
             pull(r_squared) %>%
             set_names(c("identity", "log", "sqrt", "cuberoot"))) %>%
  set_names(c("TotalSF", "LotArea", "GarageArea"))
r2 <- function(feature, transform) round(vR2[[feature]][transform], 3)

# skewness of each feature
vSkew <- map_dbl(c(TotalSF = "TotalSF", LotArea = "LotArea", GarageArea = "GarageArea"), ~ timeDate::skewness(dfClean[[.x]], na.rm = T))

What’s notable?

  • A log transform roughly doubles the R-squared of LotArea (skewness 12.8), from 0.066 to 0.138. Its few very large lots dominate a linear fit until they are compressed.
  • TotalSF (skewness 1.5) gains modestly from any of the transforms, from 0.61 to 0.647 with a log.
  • GarageArea (skewness 0.2) is barely skewed, and transforming it makes the fit worse: the R-squared drops from 0.426 to 0.389 with a log, which also has to drop the properties without a garage.
  • So only the heavily skewed features should be log transformed before fitting linear models, rather than all of them.

Correlations with SalePrice

We isolate the features that have an absolute correlation of 0.1 or more with SalePrice. Pearson correlation measures how linear a relationship is, so it is sensitive to outliers and skewed features. Spearman correlation is computed on ranks, so it measures how monotonic a relationship is. Comparing the two shows which relationships are strong but not linear:

library(corrr)

dfCor <- dfClean[vFeaturesNum] %>% 
  correlate() %>% 
  focus(SalePrice) %>% 
  dplyr::rename(feature = term,
                corr = SalePrice) %>%
  arrange(desc(abs(corr))) %>% 
  dplyr::filter(abs(corr) > 0.1) %>% 
  mutate(corr = round(corr, 2)) %>% 
  mutate(feature = fct_reorder(feature, corr)) %>% 
  dplyr::filter(!(feature %in% vFeatures_to_exclude))

vFeaturesCor <- dfCor %>% pull(feature) %>% as.character()

p1 <- eda_plot_target_correlations(dfClean[vFeaturesNum], "SalePrice", method = "pearson", minAbsCor = 0.1)
p2 <- eda_plot_target_correlations(dfClean[vFeaturesNum], "SalePrice", method = "spearman", minAbsCor = 0.1)
cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = list(p1, p2), ncol = 2)

# compare Pearson and Spearman correlations
dfCorMethods <- tibble(feature = setdiff(vFeaturesNum, "SalePrice")) %>%
  mutate(pearson = map_dbl(feature, ~ cor(dfClean[[.x]], dfClean$SalePrice, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")),
         spearman = map_dbl(feature, ~ cor(dfClean[[.x]], dfClean$SalePrice, use = "pairwise.complete.obs", method = "spearman")))
cor_of <- function(feature_name, method) round(dfCorMethods[[method]][dfCorMethods$feature == feature_name], 2)

What’s notable?

  • The top 5 features are TotalSF, GarageArea, TotalBath, TotalBsmtSF, 1stFlrSF. Quite reasonably, a buyer would look at these features to evaluate a property and its SalePrice.
  • It is somewhat counterintuitive that PropertyAge shows a strong negative correlation with SalePrice. It means properties that were more recently built, sell for higher prices than older properties.
  • Most features have similar Pearson and Spearman correlations, but LotArea stands out: its correlation rises from 0.27 to 0.43. Larger lots do sell for more, but the relationship is far from linear, which the log transform above partly addresses.
  • The opposite happens with BsmtFinSF1, whose correlation falls from 0.43 to 0.33. About 32% of the properties have no finished basement and share the same rank, while the largest finished basements carry extra weight in the Pearson correlation. So its linear relationship with SalePrice looks stronger than its rank relationship.

Numerical-Categorical (Ordinal)

cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist=map2(vFeaturesCat1,"SalePrice", ~ eda_plot_box(dfClean, .x, .y, yLimits = c(35000,410000))), ncol = 4)

What’s notable?

  • We can spot clear trends in SalePrice v/s the order of the categories in almost all of these features.
  • Overall quality and external quality show some of the strongest trends.

Numerical-Categorical (Nominal)

Let’s examine SalePrice with respect to the nominal features in the dataset. None of these features have a natural order, but we can identify trends within categories by sorting with the median SalePrice. The SalePrice axis is truncated to exclude outliers.

cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist=map2(vFeaturesCat2,"SalePrice", ~ eda_plot_box(dfClean, .x, .y, yLimits = c(35000,410000))), ncol = 4)

What’s notable?

  • GarageType: Builtin and attached garages are more preferred than detached or other types of garages.
  • From MSSubClass categories, it is evident that 1946 or newer houses are higher priced than older houses.

Multivariate Analysis

We will check variation of some related features with SalePrice.

Numerical-Numerical-Categorical

We have determined TotalSF and GarageArea have among the strongest correlations with SalePrice. Let’s see how they vary by NeighborhoodType and GarageType respectively:

p1 <- eda_plot_scatter_cat(dfClean, "TotalSF", "SalePrice", "NeighborhoodType", yLabelsScale = scales::dollar)
p2 <- eda_plot_scatter_cat(dfClean, "GarageArea", "SalePrice", "GarageType", yLabelsScale = scales::dollar)
cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = list(p1, p2), ncol = 1)

  • For the same total area, there are neighborhoods where SalePrice is higher than others.
  • Properties with no garage are distinctly separated.
  • Properties with built-in or attached garages tend to have higher SalePrice for the same GarageArea.
  • Therefore, NeighborhoodType and GarageType explain some variance in SalePrice.

Categorical-Numerical-Numerical

The scatterplots overlap a lot, so let’s check these observations by comparing categories among properties of similar size. TotalSF and GarageArea are split into four quartile bins, and SalePrice is plotted by category within each bin. We also check whether central air conditioning (CentralAir) matters for properties of the same size:

p1 <- eda_plot_box_by_bins(dfClean, "NeighborhoodType", "SalePrice", "TotalSF", yLog = T, yLabelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1))
p2 <- eda_plot_box_by_bins(dfClean, "GarageType", "SalePrice", "GarageArea", yLog = T, yLabelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1))
p3 <- eda_plot_box_by_bins(dfClean, "CentralAir", "SalePrice", "TotalSF", yLog = T, yLabelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1))
cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = list(p1, p2, p3), ncol = 1)

# median SalePrice by category within each bin
get_bin_medians <- function(p) {
  p$data %>%
    group_by(bin = as.integer(bin), category = as.character(x)) %>%
    summarise(median = median(y), .groups = "drop")
}
lBinMedians <- map(list(neighborhood = p1, garage = p2, air = p3), get_bin_medians)
bin_median <- function(plotName, binNum, categoryName) {
  dfMedians <- lBinMedians[[plotName]]
  scales::dollar(dfMedians$median[dfMedians$bin == binNum & dfMedians$category == categoryName], accuracy = 1)
}

What’s notable?

  • Neighborhood matters a lot even for properties of the same size. Among the largest properties, the median SalePrice ranges from $161,000 in Type5 neighborhoods to $327,000 in Type1 neighborhoods. Type1 neighborhoods have few or no properties in the smallest bin, so neighborhood and size are related too.
  • For the same GarageArea, built-in and attached garages are associated with higher prices than detached ones. Among the largest garages, the median SalePrice is $299,018 for built-in, $253,000 for attached and $140,000 for detached garages. Some garage types have very few properties, so their boxplots are less reliable.
  • Properties with central air conditioning sell for more at every size. Among the largest properties, the median SalePrice is $262,140 with central air and $136,000 without it.

Categorical-Categorical-Numerical

We want to see if there is any interaction of SalePrice with a combination of categorical features, that could provide any additional explanatory power for prediction:

p1 <- eda_plot_heatmap(dfClean, "OverallQual", "NeighborhoodType", "SalePrice")
p2 <- eda_plot_heatmap(dfClean, "GarageType", "NeighborhoodType", "SalePrice")
p3 <- eda_plot_heatmap(dfClean, "MSSubClass", "MSZoning", "SalePrice")
cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = list(p1, p2, p3), ncol = 1)

  • It is evident that some neighborhoods have higher OverallQual and therefore command higher price. However in Type4 neighborhoods, we can see a clear variation in SalePrice by quality of property.
  • It is less clear if GarageType has a major impact by itself. Even though built-in and attached garages seem to be preferred, most of the variation can be explained by NeighborhoodType itself.
  • Low density and floating village residential properties tend to be higher priced in both single and multi-storied properties built after 1946.
# split the data back to training and testing sets
# dfTrain <- dfClean %>% dplyr::slice(1:nrows_train)
# dfTest <- dfClean %>% dplyr::slice(-(1:nrows_train))

save(vFeaturesCat, vFeaturesNum, vFeaturesCor, dfClean, vTestIDs, 
     file = "Ames_Housing_Clean.Rda")

item.title: Diamonds - Part 3 - A polished gem - Building Non-linear Models
item.description:
Other posts in this series:

  • Diamonds - Part 1 - In the rough - An Exploratory Data Analysis
  • Diamonds - Part 2 - A cut above - Building Linear Models

In a couple of previous posts, we tried to understand what attributes of diamonds are important to determine their prices. We showed that carat, clarity and color are the most important predictors of price. We arrived at this conclusion after doing a detailed exploratory data analysis. Finally we fit linear models to predict prices and determined the best model from the metrics.

In this post, we will use non-linear regression models to predict diamond prices and compare them with those from linear models.

Training Non-linear Models

We’ll follow some of the same steps as we did for linear models, while transforming some predictors:

  • Partition the dataset into training and testing sets in the proportion 75% and 25% respectively.
  • Stratify the partitioning by clarity, so both training and testing sets have the same distributions of this feature.
  • clarity, color and cut have ordered categories from lowest to highest grades. The randomForest method requires no change in representing this data before training the models, however xgboost and keras methods require all the predictors to be in numerical form. Two methods could be used for transforming the categorical data:
    1. Use one-hot encoding to convert categorical data to sparse data with 0s and 1s. This way, each category in clarity, color and cut is converted to a new predictor in binary form. A disadvantage of this method is that it treates ordered categorical data the same as unordered categorical data, so the ordinality is lost in transformation. However, non-linear models should be able to infer the ordinality as our training sample is sufficiently large.
    2. Represent the ordinal categories from lowest to highest grades in integer form. However, this creates a linear gradation from one category to another, which may not be a suitable choice here.
  • Center and scale all values in the training set and build a matrix of predictors.
  • Fit a non-linear model with the training set.
  • Make predictions on the testing set and determine model metrics.
  • Wrap all the steps above inside a function in which the model formula, and a seed could be passed that randomizes the partition of training and testing sets.
  • Run multiple iterations of models with different seeds, and compute their average metrics, that would reflect results on unseen data.

Here are the average metrics for all the models trained with keras, randomForest and xgboost regression methods:

load("fit_models_keras.Rda")

dfModels_keras <- dfModels %>% mutate(type = "keras")
best_model_results_keras <- best_model_results
dfResults_keras <- best_model_results_keras$dfResults %>% mutate(type = "keras")

load("fit_models_rf.Rda")

dfModels_rf <- dfModels %>% mutate(type = "randomForest")
best_model_results_rf <- best_model_results
dfResults_rf <- best_model_results_rf$dfResults %>% mutate(type = "randomForest")

load("fit_models_xgb.Rda")

dfModels_xgb <- dfModels %>% mutate(type = "xgboost")
best_model_results_xgb <- best_model_results
dfResults_xgb <- best_model_results_xgb$dfResults %>% mutate(type = "xgboost")

# combine the actual v/s predicted results from the best model using the 3 methods
dfResults <- map_df(list(dfResults_keras, dfResults_rf, dfResults_xgb), bind_rows) %>% 
  select(type, everything()) %>% 
  mutate_if(is.numeric, ~ round(.x, digits = 2)) %>% 
  group_by(type)

# combine the average metrics from all the models using the 3 methods
dfModels <- map_df(list(dfModels_keras, dfModels_rf, dfModels_xgb), bind_rows) %>% 
  select(type, everything()) %>% 
  mutate_if(is.numeric, ~ round(.x, digits = 2)) %>% 
  gather(avg_metric, value, rmse, rsq, mae)

# create an HTML table
dfModels %>% tidyHtmlTable(header = "type", cgroup1 = "avg_metric", cell_value = "value", rnames = "model", align = "|rrr|rrr|rrr")
keras randomForest xgboost
price ~ . c(“989.71”, “0.93”, “360.55”) c(“529.28”, “0.98”, “262.35”) c(“540.76”, “0.98”, “280.49”)
price ~ carat c(“1499.2”, “0.86”, “860.29”) c(“1427.25”, “0.87”, “816.1”) c(“1427.35”, “0.87”, “815.76”)
price ~ carat + clarity c(“1040.69”, “0.93”, “590.32”) c(“1006.61”, “0.94”, “548.67”) c(“992.46”, “0.94”, “544.48”)
price ~ carat + clarity + color c(“645.4”, “0.97”, “358.85”) c(“571.73”, “0.98”, “305.17”) c(“575.3”, “0.98”, “306.86”)
price ~ carat + clarity + color + cut c(“626.78”, “0.98”, “347.99”) c(“545.02”, “0.98”, “285.96”) c(“541.63”, “0.98”, “282.38”)

Looking at the r-squared terms, it is remarkable how well all the models have been able to infer the complex relationship between price and carat. To fit linear models, we needed to transform both price and carat to logarithmic terms. The neural network as well as the decision tree based models do this all on their own. The root mean squared error is in $ terms so it is easier to interpret. Considering the mean and standard deviation of price in the dataset is about $4000, the root mean squared errors of the models are very low. With carat, clarity and color, they range from $572 to $645, compared with about $816 for the best linear model with the same predictors.

Exploratory data analysis adds value here, as the models with carat, clarity and color give excellent results. Including cut in the models does not provide any significant benefits and results in overfitted models.

Even the base models with all predictors: price ~ . (where some of them are confounders), do a very good job of explaning the variance. Decision tree and neural network models are unaffected by multi-collinearity. We can use local model interpretations to determine the most important predictors from these models.

Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations

LIME is a method for explaining black-box machine learning models. It can help visualize and explain individual predictions. It makes the assumption that every complex model is linear on a local scale. So it is possible to fit a simple model around a single observation that will behave how the global model behaves at that locality. The simple model can be used to explain the predictions of the more complex model locally.

The generalized algorithm LIME applies is:

  • Given an observation, permute it to create replicated feature data with slight value modifications.
  • Compute similarity distance measure between original observation and permuted observations.
  • Apply selected machine learning model to predict outcomes of permuted data.
  • Select m number of features to best describe predicted outcomes.
  • Fit a simple model to the permuted data, explaining the complex model outcome with m features from the permuted data weighted by its similarity to the original observation .
  • Use the resulting feature weights to explain local behavior.

Here we will select 5 features that best describe the predicted outcomes for 6 random observations from the testing set.

# Plot Feature Importance by sample
plot_features(explanation_keras, ncol = 3) + 
  labs(title = "LIME Feature Importance from a keras model",
       subtitle = glue::glue("{numSamples} random samples from testing set")) +
  theme_quant() +
  theme(plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

plot_features(explanation_xgb, ncol = 3) + 
  labs(title = "LIME Feature Importance from an xgboost model",
       subtitle = glue::glue("{numSamples} random samples from testing set")) +
  theme_quant() +
  theme(plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

The features by importance that best explain the predictions in these 6 random samples are carat, clarity, color, x and y.

# Plot Feature Importance Heatmap
plot_explanations(explanation_keras) +
  labs(title = "LIME Feature Importance Heatmap from a keras model",
       subtitle = glue::glue("{numSamples} random samples from testing set")) +
  theme_quant() +
  theme(plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

plot_explanations(explanation_xgb) +
  labs(title = "LIME Feature Importance Heatmap from an xgboost model",
       subtitle = glue::glue("{numSamples} random samples from testing set")) +
  theme_quant() +
  theme(plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

We know that x and y are co-linear with carat, which is why it is good practice to remove any redundant features from the training data before applying any machine learning algorithm. We find the model with the best metrics turns out to be the one using carat, clarity and color.

Actual v/s Predicted

Finally, here are the scatterplots of actual v/s predicted price from the best model on the testing set, using the 3 regression methods:

p1 <- dfResults %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  rename(price = actual) %>%
  eda_plot_actual_vs_predicted("price", "estimate", feature_model = "type", nLabel = 0,
                               labelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(title = paste(formulaString_best, "(linear scale)")) +
  theme(panel.spacing.x = unit(2, "lines"), plot.margin = margin(5, 25, 5, 5))

p2 <- dfResults %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  rename(price = actual) %>%
  eda_plot_actual_vs_predicted("price", "estimate", feature_model = "type", nLabel = 0, xLog = T, yLog = T,
                               labelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(title = paste(formulaString_best, "(log scale)")) +
  theme(panel.spacing.x = unit(2, "lines"), plot.margin = margin(5, 25, 5, 5))

cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = list(p1, p2), ncol = 1)

The scatterplots are shown with both linear and logarithmic axes. Even though the results from all the 3 methods have roughly similar r-squared and rmse values, we can see predicted prices from keras have more dispersion than the two decision-tree methods at the higher end. The decision-tree based methods appear do a better job of predicting prices at the lower end with lesser dispersion.

As in the case with linear models, the variance in predicted diamond prices increases with price. The decision-tree based methods keep their predictions close to the range of prices in the data: their highest predictions are $18,340 (randomForest) and $19,118 (xgboost), while the most expensive diamond in the testing set costs $18,823. A randomForest prediction is an average of prices seen in the training data, so it cannot go beyond them, and xgboost adds up many small corrections, so it can exceed them only slightly. A neural network, like a linear model, can extrapolate further, and the highest price predicted by keras is $26,591. So, not only do non-linear methods do a fantastic job in inferring the relationships between price and its predictors, the decision-tree methods also predict prices within a reasonable range.

Summary

  • All the 3 non-linear regression methods can infer the complex relationship between price, carat and other predictors, without the need for feature engineering.
  • Exploratory Data Analysis is useful in removing the redundant features from the training dataset, resulting in both faster execution, as well as much better metrics.
  • In terms of time taken to train the models, keras neural network models execute the fastest by virtue of being able to use GPUs.
  • Among the decision-tree based methods, xgboost models train much faster than randomForest models.
  • Multiple CPUs can be used to run randomForest and xgboost methods. RAM is the only limiting constraint, when trained on a local machine.

item.description:
In a previous post in this series, we did an exploratory data analysis of the diamonds dataset and found that carat, x, y, z were strongly correlated with price, and that log(price) was close to linear in log(carat). For diamonds of similar weight, clarity and color also appeared to provide some predictive ability.

In this post, we will build linear models and see how well they predict the price of diamonds.

Before we do any transformations, feature engineering or feature selections for our model, let’s see what kind of results we get from a base linear model, that uses all the features to predict price:

The model summary shows it is an overfitted model. Among other things, we know that depth and table have no impact on price, yet these are shown to be highly significant. Root Mean Squared Error (rmse) and other metrics are also shown above.

Let’s make a plot of actual v/s predicted prices to visualize how well this base model performs.

  eda_plot_actual_vs_predicted("price", ".fitted", nLabel = 0, labelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)) +

If the predictions are good, the points should lie close to a straight line drawn at 45 degrees. We can see this base model does a poor job of predicting prices. Worst of all, the model predicts negative prices on the lower end. It shows that price has to be log transformed to avoid these absurdities.

Feature Engineering

We know the price of a diamond is strongly correlated with its size. All things equal, the larger the diamond, the greater its price.

As a first approximation, we can assume a diamond is a cuboid with dimensions x, y and z. Then, we can compute its volume as x * y * z. As these 3 dimensions are highly correlated, we can compute a geometrical average dimension by taking the cube root of volume, and retain a linear relationship with log(price).

Another way to calculate an average dimension is by using high school chemistry. Mass, volume and density are related to each other by the equation:

$ density = mass/volume $

We can find out that 1 carat = 0.2 gms. Dividing by the density of diamond (3.51 gms/cc) would give us its volume in cc, which could be converted to a geometrical average dimension by taking the cube root.

dfInput <- diamonds %>% 
  mutate(volume = x*y*z,
         `average dimension` = volume ^ (1/3),
         volume2 = carat * 0.2/3.51,
         `average dimension2` = (volume2 ^ (1/3)) * 10)   # Multiply by 10 to convert from cm to mm

eda_plot_scatter(dfInput, c("average dimension", "average dimension2"), "price", yLabelsScale = scales::dollar) + 
  labs(title = "Scatterplot of price v/s average dimension")

Even though both methods yield similar results, we could see that the density method results in a narrower range. But which method would be more robust? Keep in mind there are 20 z values that are 0. In 7 of these records both x and y are 0 too, which means these values were not recorded reliably.

In all of these records, the carat values were recorded reliably and are probably more accurate than the dimensions. Hence, we might prefer the density method of generating this feature.

Furthermore, since density is a constant, dividing by a constant to calculate volume isn’t really necessary. Instead, a cube root transformation could be applied to carat itself for the purposes of predictive modelling that would result in a linear relationship between \(log(price)\) and \(carat^{1/3}\). It is the reason why we’re fitting a linear model because the model is linear in its parameters.

The geometric argument favours a cube root, but is it the transform that makes the relationship most linear? Let’s compare it with others, labelling each panel with the R-squared of a linear fit of log(price):

p_transforms <- eda_plot_transforms(diamonds, "carat", "price")
p_transforms

# R-squared of each transform, in the order of the panels
vR2_carat <- p_transforms$data %>%
  distinct(transform, r_squared) %>%
  pull(r_squared) %>%
  set_names(c("identity", "log", "sqrt", "cuberoot"))

The cube root (R-squared 0.924) is a big improvement on untransformed carat (0.847), but log(carat) does even better (0.933). A linear relationship between \(log(price)\) and \(log(carat)\) has a simple interpretation: the coefficient of \(log(carat)\) is the percentage change in price for a 1% change in carat. We will try both transforms in our models.

Training Linear Models

Here are the steps for building linear models and computing metrics:

  • Partition the dataset into training and testing sets in the proportion 75% and 25% respectively.
  • Since clarity is one of the main predictors, stratify the partitioning by clarity, so both training and testing sets have the same distributions of this feature.
  • Fit a linear model with the training set.
  • Make predictions on the testing set and determine model metrics.
  • Wrap all the steps above inside a function in which the model formula and a seed could be passed. Since the seed determines the random partitioning, it helps to minimize vagaries in partitioning the training and testing sets before fitting models.
  • Run multiple iterations of a model with different seeds, and compute its average metrics, that would reflect the results on unseen data.

Here’s a sample split of training and testing set, stratified by clarity. As we can see, the training and testing sets have similar distributions.

set.seed(1333)
train_split <- diamonds %>% 
  select(price, everything()) %>% 
  initial_split(prop = 0.75, strata = "clarity")

dfTrain <- training(train_split)
dfTest <- testing(train_split)

fit_linear_model <- function(randomSeed, model_formula, get_model = FALSE) {

  set.seed(randomSeed)
  train_split <- diamonds %>% 
    select(price, everything()) %>% 
    initial_split(prop = 0.75, strata = "clarity")
  
  dfTrain <- training(train_split)
  dfTest <- testing(train_split)

  # fit a linear model
  model_lm <- lm(model_formula, data = dfTrain)
  
  # predict on testing set to determine rmse  
  predict_lm <- predict(model_lm, dfTest)

  # predict on testing set with outliers
  dfResults <- dfTest %>% 
    mutate(actual = price) %>% 
    mutate(estimate = predict_lm %>% exp()) %>% 
    select(actual, estimate)
  
  if(get_model) {
    return(list(model_lm, dfResults))
  } else {
    return(dfResults)
  }
}

dfModels <- expand_grid(seed = vRandomSeeds, 
                        model = c("log(price) ~ .",
                                  "log(price) ~ I(carat^(1/3))",

  unnest(cols = metrics) %>%

Univariate Analysis

Let us look at each feature in the dataset in detail.

Numerical Features

The plots show presence of outliers within each feature. Let’s exclude the outliers and plot them again.

makeOutliersNA <- function(Z) {
  min_value = min(Z, na.rm = T)
  max_value = max(Z, na.rm = T)
  median_value = median(Z, na.rm = T)
  IQR = IQR(Z, na.rm = T)
  lower_bound = max(min_value, median_value - 2.5*IQR)
  upper_bound = min(max_value, median_value + 2.5*IQR)
  
  Z <- ifelse(Z >= lower_bound & Z <= upper_bound, Z, NA)
}

# convert outliers to NA values
dfInput <- dfInput %>% mutate_at(vFeaturesNum, makeOutliersNA)

eda_plot_histograms(dfInput, vFeaturesNum) + labs(title = "Histograms of numerical features excluding outliers")

Let’s plot the distribution of price in log scale:

eda_plot_histograms(dfInput, "price", nBins = 100, xLog = T, xLabelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1))

Two peaks in the log transformed plot show a bimodal distribution of prices. This implies two price points of diamonds are most popular among customers - one at just below USD 1000 and the other around USD 5000. Intriguingly, there are no diamonds in the dataset that are around USD 1500. Hence, a big gap is visible around that price.

Categorical Features

cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = map(vFeaturesCat, ~ eda_plot_column(dfInput, .x)), ncol = 2)

The categorical imbalance in cut and clarity can be clearly noticed.

Bivariate Analysis

Let’s examine the relationship of price with other features.

Numerical-numerical

First and foremost, let’s do a correlation analysis to see how price is correlated with other numerical features:

eda_plot_correlation_matrix(dfInput[vFeaturesNum] %>% drop_na(), outlineVar = "price", plotTitle = "Clustered correlations of numerical features")

We can see that price is very strongly correlated with carat, x, y, and z dimensions. If a predictive linear regression model is built, some of these features would act as confounders. table and depth have almost no correlation with price so they are not so interesting for predictive modelling.

Now let’s see the scatter plots:

eda_plot_scatter(dfInput, vFeaturesNum, "price", yLimits = c(200, 15000), yLabelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1))

After removing outliers, it could be noted that price increases exponentially with carat, as well as x, y and z dimensions. So price should be plotted with a log tranformation. Let’s do that:

eda_plot_scatter(dfInput, vFeaturesNum, "price", yLog = T, yLimits = c(200, 15000), yLabelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1))

Now, the relationship between log(price) appears to be linear with x, y and z. But, not so much with carat. Variance in price tends to increase both by carat and its dimensions.

Which transform of carat would make its relationship with log(price) linear? Let’s compare a few common transforms. Each panel is labelled with the R-squared of a linear fit of log(price) on the transformed carat:

p_transforms <- eda_plot_transforms(dfInput, "carat", "price")
p_transforms

# R-squared of each transform, in the order of the panels
vR2_carat <- p_transforms$data %>%
  distinct(transform, r_squared) %>%
  pull(r_squared) %>%
  set_names(c("identity", "log", "sqrt", "cuberoot"))

log(carat) makes the relationship the most linear, with an R-squared of 0.926, followed by the cube root (0.919) and the square root (0.91). Untransformed carat has the lowest R-squared of 0.862. So log(price) is close to linear in log(carat): a given percentage increase in weight raises the price by a roughly constant percentage. We will make use of this when we do Feature Engineering.

Numerical-Categorical

Let’s examine price with respect to the categorical features in the dataset:

cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = map(vFeaturesCat, ~ eda_plot_box(dfInput, .x, "price", yLimits = c(300, 8000), 
                                                               yLabelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1))), ncol = 3)

The boxplots above are plotted with truncated price axis for better visualization of trends. All the boxplots are counter-intuitive - median prices tend to decline as we move from lowest grade to highest grade in terms of cut, color and clarity. This is very odd. We will find out why in the multivariate analysis.

  • The median price declines monotonically from Fair cut to Ideal cut.
  • In terms of color, the median price decreases from J (worst) to G (mid-grade), then increases and finally decreases for D (best).
  • The median price increases when clarity improves from I1 to SI2, and then decreases monotonically to IF grade.

Multivariate Analysis

So far, we have determined carat, x, y, and z have the strongest relationship with price. Different grades of cut, color and clarity also seem to have some impact on median price. So let’s make some scatter plots to see these relationships:

Numerical-Numerical-Categorical

cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = map(vFeaturesCat, ~ eda_plot_scatter_cat(dfInput, "carat", "price", .x, yLabelsScale = scales::dollar)), ncol = 2)

Although there is a lot of overlap, but there is a clear trend of price increasing with clarity, at a given carat weight. The same pattern could also be observed in the plot with increasing grades of color, though not to the same extent. There is no evidence of any relationship between price and carat with cut.

We can conclude both color and clarity explain some variance in price at a given carat weight.

Categorical-Numerical-Numerical

The overlap in the scatterplots makes it hard to see how much each grade matters. Let’s compare the grades among diamonds of similar weight, by splitting carat into four quartile bins and plotting price by grade within each bin:

lBinPlots <- map(c("clarity", "color", "cut"), ~ eda_plot_box_by_bins(dfInput, .x, "price", "carat", yLog = T,
                                                                       yLabelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)))
cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = lBinPlots, ncol = 1)

# median price by grade within each carat bin
get_bin_medians <- function(p) {
  p$data %>%
    group_by(bin = as.integer(bin), grade = as.character(x)) %>%
    summarise(median = median(y), .groups = "drop")
}
dfBinMedians_clarity <- get_bin_medians(lBinPlots[[1]])
bin_median <- function(dfMedians, binNum, gradeName) {
  scales::dollar(dfMedians$median[dfMedians$bin == binNum & dfMedians$grade == gradeName], accuracy = 1)
}

# median carat by clarity
dfCarat_clarity <- dfInput %>% group_by(clarity) %>% summarise(carat = median(carat, na.rm = T))

This resolves the paradox in the boxplots of the bivariate analysis:

  • Within each carat bin, the median price generally rises with clarity, most clearly among the heaviest diamonds, where it goes from $3,985 for I1 to $10,332 for IF. The top grades (VVS2 to IF) are priced close to each other and not always in order.
  • price also rises with color from J to G within each bin, but the top grades (G to D) are priced about the same. Among the heaviest diamonds, D and E are even slightly cheaper than G.
  • cut shows no consistent trend, even among diamonds of similar weight.

The reason better grades look cheaper overall is that they tend to be smaller. The median weight of an I1 diamond is 1.07 carat, but only 0.35 carat for an IF diamond. carat confounds the relationship between price and the grades, so it has to be accounted for when we judge the effect of clarity or color.

To be sure of any interaction between table and depth, with color and clarity, let’s plot these:

dfFeatures <- expand_grid(feat1 = c("depth","table"), feat2 = c("color","clarity")) %>% arrange(desc(feat2))
cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = map2(dfFeatures$feat1, dfFeatures$feat2, 
                                   ~ eda_plot_scatter_cat(dfInput, .x, "price", .y, yLabelsScale = scales::dollar)), nrow = 2)

There is no pattern in the interaction of price v/s depth and table values when plotted by color and clarity. So, these features do not have any predictive ability to determine price.

Categorical-Categorical-Numerical

We want to see if there is any interaction of clarity with cut and color, that could provide any additional explanatory power to predict price:

cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = map(c("cut","color"), ~ eda_plot_heatmap(dfInput, .x, "clarity", "price")), nrow = 2)

The second heatmap appears to be more interesting. From bottom left to top right, with increasing grades of color and clarity, price tends to decrease on average. Once again, this runs counter to our intuition; after all prices of diamonds with the best color and clarity should be the highest. Nevertheless this counter-trend persists in the dataset.

With respect to cut and clarity, the mean prices do not show any discernable pattern.

Summary

To summarize, here’s what we found interesting in this dataset, after doing an exploratory data analysis:

  • price is heavily right-skewed, and when log tranformed, has a bimodal distribution which implies there is demand in 2 different price ranges.
  • carat about 75% of the diamonds are below 1 carat. The variance in price increases with carat weight, and log(price) is close to linear in log(carat).
  • cut is imbalanced with about 40% of the diamonds rated Ideal.
  • color is imbalanced with about 5% of the diamonds rated J.
  • clarity is imbalanced at the extremes, with only 1.5% of the diamonds rated I1 and 3.3% of the diamonds rated IF.
  • price is strongly correlated with carat and x, y, z dimensions of the diamonds. table and depth have almost no correlation with price.
  • Both clarity and color explain some variance in price for a given carat weight. Their apparent negative effect on price overall is because diamonds of better grades tend to be smaller. cut has little effect.
